title: Jurgen Habermas

cards.b:
Jurgen Habermas (born 1929), the leading figure of the second-generation Frankfurt School, defends reason and democracy against both Marxist pessimism and postmodern doubt. He gave us the public sphere, communicative action and deliberative democracy, themes often in Paper I.

Expect this as a 10 or 15 mark question, or as a supporting example inside a longer answer. Read the cards in order, then test yourself with the quiz.

In The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962) Habermas traces the rise of the 18th-century bourgeois public sphere: coffee houses, salons and the press, where private people debated state affairs by reason. Later, mass media, advertising and the welfare state turned citizens into consumers and the public into a managed audience. He calls for its revival.

The Theory of Communicative Action (1981) distinguishes two kinds of rationality.

  • Instrumental (strategic): reason used to reach goals, to manipulate.
  • Communicative: reason used to reach mutual understanding through argument.

Speech always carries validity claims: truth, rightness, sincerity and comprehensibility. We can test them with reasons.
Modernity's pathology: the system colonises the lifeworld, so that money and administrative power invade areas that should run on dialogue (health, education, family).

A norm is valid only if all affected could accept it in a practical discourse free from coercion. The ideal speech situation is a regulative ideal: equal chance to speak, no force except the force of the better argument. It is a test for real-world talk, not a description of it.

In Between Facts and Norms (1992) he gives a two-track model: informal opinion formation in civil society (the wild public sphere) feeds formal institutions such as parliament and courts, which turn it into law. Law and popular sovereignty, rights and democracy, 'co-originate'. He also proposed constitutional patriotism: loyalty to constitutional principles instead of ethnic nation.

• Foucault, Lyotard: reason hides power. Habermas answers: the postmodern is a performative contradiction, and modernity is an 'unfinished project'.
  • Nancy Fraser: his bourgeois public excluded women and workers, who made 'counter-publics'.
  • Mouffe: consensus ignores conflict, so use agonism.
  • Rawls: 1995 debate over proceduralism; Rawls adds 'reasonable pluralism'.
  • Too demanding and utopian.

Adorno and Horkheimer, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944), saw reason as turned into domination. Habermas replies that instrumental reason is only one side of reason and that communicative reason carries emancipation. His Legitimation Crisis (1973) warns that late capitalism faces a crisis when citizens no longer accept its justification.

Habermasian ideas are useful for studying the press, RTI Act (2005), social audits, gram sabhas and Constituent Assembly debates. Amartya Sen's The Argumentative Indian (2005) highlights India's tradition of public reasoning. Modern worries: fake news, polarised social media and hate speech, which damage the quality of public debate.
